Reinhard Genzel studies [infrared-](/wiki/Infrared_astronomy "Infrared astronomy") and [submillimetre astronomy](/wiki/Submillimetre_astronomy "Submillimetre astronomy"). He and his group are
active in developing ground- and space-based instruments for astronomy. They used these to track the motions of stars at the centre of the [Milky Way](/wiki/Milky_Way "Milky Way"), around [Sagittarius A\*](/wiki/Sagittarius_A* "Sagittarius A*"), and show that they were orbiting a very massive object, now known to be a [black hole](/wiki/Black_hole "Black hole").[[9]](#cite_note-9) Genzel is also active in studies of the formation and evolution of galaxies.[[7]](#cite_note-UC_Berkeley_Physics-7)

In July 2018, Reinhard Genzel *et al.* reported that [star S2](/wiki/S2_(star) "S2 (star)") orbiting Sgr A\* had been recorded at 7,650 km/s or 2.55% the speed of light leading up to the [pericentre](/wiki/Pericentre "Pericentre") approach in May 2018 at about 120 [AU](/wiki/Astronomical_unit "Astronomical unit") ≈ 1400 [Schwarzschild radii](/wiki/Schwarzschild_radius "Schwarzschild radius") from Sgr A\*. This allowed them to test the [redshift](/wiki/Redshift "Redshift") predicted by [general relativity](/wiki/General_relativity "General relativity") at [relativistic velocities](/wiki/Relativistic_velocities "Relativistic velocities"), finding additional confirmation of the theory.[[10]](#cite_note-aa33718-18-10)[[11]](#cite_note-2017-07-26_TG-11)

In 2008, amongst women, [breast cancer](/wiki/Breast_cancer "Breast cancer") was the most commonly occurring cancer, with about 25% of cancer diagnoses. In 2008, cancer was responsible for about 25% of all US deaths. The statistics below are estimates for the U.S. in 2008, and may vary substantially in other countries. They exclude basal and squamous cell skin cancers, and [carcinoma in situ](/wiki/Carcinoma_in_situ "Carcinoma in situ") in locations other than the urinary bladder.[[22]](#cite_note-Jemal-22) As seen, breast/prostate cancer, lung cancer and colorectal cancer are responsible for approximately half of cancer incidence. The same applies for cancer mortality, but with lung cancer replacing breast/prostate cancer as the main cause.

In 1998, the [International Agency for Research on Cancer](/wiki/International_Agency_for_Research_on_Cancer "International Agency for Research on Cancer") (Centre International de Recherche sur le Cancer) of the [World Health Organization](/wiki/World_Health_Organization "World Health Organization") classified alcoholic beverages as a [carcinogen](/wiki/Carcinogen "Carcinogen"). Its evaluation states:[[19]](#cite_note-19)

> There is sufficient evidence for the carcinogenicity of alcoholic beverages in humans. […] Alcoholic beverages are carcinogenic to humans ([Group 1](/wiki/IARC_group_1_Carcinogens "IARC group 1 Carcinogens")).

After more [epidemiological](/wiki/Epidemiology "Epidemiology") evidence connecting alcohol and cancers became available, the IARC reconvened in 2007. Based on epidemiological studies, which revealed cancer risk was independent of the type of alcohol, and animal studies, which showed increased cancer risk with exposure to ethanol alone, the group determined that the ethanol in alcoholic beverages was carcinogenic to humans. Alcohol was determined to increase the risk of developing breast cancer, liver cancer, colorectal cancer, esophageal cancers, pharyngeal cancer, laryngeal cancer, and oral cancer. In 2009, the group determined that acetaldehyde which is a metabolite of ethanol is also carcinogenic to humans.[[20]](#cite_note-20)

*[Deschampsia antarctica](/wiki/Deschampsia_antarctica "Deschampsia antarctica")* at [Collins Glacier](/wiki/Collins_Glacier "Collins Glacier"), Antarctica. This species is one of only two flowering plants native to Antarctica, the other one being Antarctic pearlwort (Colobanthus quitensis).

Throughout its history, Antarctica has seen a wide variety of plant life. In the [Cretaceous](/wiki/Cretaceous "Cretaceous"), it was dominated by a fern-[conifer](/wiki/Conifer "Conifer") ecosystem, which changed into a temperate [rainforest](/wiki/Rainforest "Rainforest") by the end of that period. During the colder [Neogene](/wiki/Neogene "Neogene") (17–2.5 Ma), a [tundra](/wiki/Tundra "Tundra") ecosystem replaced the rainforests. The climate of present-day Antarctica does not allow extensive vegetation to form.[[134]](#cite_note-137) A combination of freezing temperatures, poor [soil quality](/wiki/Soil_quality "Soil quality"), and a lack of moisture and sunlight inhibit plant growth, causing low [species diversity](/wiki/Species_diversity "Species diversity") and limited distribution. The [flora](/wiki/Flora "Flora") largely consists of [bryophytes](/wiki/Bryophyte "Bryophyte") (25 species of [liverworts](/wiki/Marchantiophyta "Marchantiophyta") and 100 species of [mosses](/wiki/Moss "Moss")). There are three species of [flowering plants](/wiki/Flowering_plant "Flowering plant"), all of which are found in the Antarctic Peninsula: *[Deschampsia antarctica](/wiki/Deschampsia_antarctica "Deschampsia antarctica")* (Antarctic hair grass), *[Colobanthus quitensis](/wiki/Colobanthus_quitensis "Colobanthus quitensis")* (Antarctic pearlwort) and the non-native *[Poa annua](/wiki/Poa_annua "Poa annua")* (annual bluegrass).[[135]](#cite_note-138)

Mandarin varieties are natively spoken by 70 percent of all Chinese speakers, spread over a large geographical area that stretches from [Yunnan](/wiki/Yunnan "Yunnan") in the southwest to [Xinjiang](/wiki/Xinjiang "Xinjiang") in the northwest and [Heilongjiang](/wiki/Heilongjiang "Heilongjiang") in the northeast. Its spread is generally attributed to the overall greater ease of travel in the [North China Plain](/wiki/North_China_Plain "North China Plain") compared to the more mountainous south, combined with the relatively recent spread of northern varieties to frontier areas.
Many varieties of Mandarin, such as [those of the Southwest](/wiki/Southwestern_Mandarin "Southwestern Mandarin") and the [Lower Yangtze](/wiki/Jianghuai_Mandarin "Jianghuai Mandarin"), are not [mutually intelligible](/wiki/Mutually_intelligible "Mutually intelligible") with the [Beijing dialect](/wiki/Beijing_dialect "Beijing dialect"). "**Since U Been Gone**" is a song recorded by American singer [Kelly Clarkson](/wiki/Kelly_Clarkson "Kelly Clarkson") from her second studio album, *[Breakaway](/wiki/Breakaway_(Kelly_Clarkson_album) "Breakaway (Kelly Clarkson album)")* (2004). The song, written and produced by [Max Martin](/wiki/Max_Martin "Max Martin") and [Lukasz "Dr. Luke" Gottwald](/wiki/Dr._Luke "Dr. Luke"), was released as the lead single from *Breakaway* two weeks before the album was released. An [uptempo](/wiki/Uptempo "Uptempo") [power ballad](/wiki/Power_ballad "Power ballad") with [alternative rock](/wiki/Alternative_rock "Alternative rock") and [indie rock](/wiki/Indie_rock "Indie rock") influences, it mixes loud and soft [pop rock](/wiki/Pop_rock "Pop rock"), [power pop](/wiki/Power_pop "Power pop"), [bubblegum](/wiki/Bubblegum_music "Bubblegum music"), and [pop-punk](/wiki/Pop-punk "Pop-punk") with [electronic](/wiki/Electronic_music "Electronic music") sounds. Martin originally wrote "Since U Been Gone" with [Pink](/wiki/Pink_(singer) "Pink (singer)") in mind, but she turned it down. It was then given to [Hilary Duff](/wiki/Hilary_Duff "Hilary Duff"), but she rejected the song because she could not reach its higher notes. The song was finally given to Clarkson after [Clive Davis](/wiki/Clive_Davis "Clive Davis") convinced the writers to give it to her. Clarkson decided to add heavier guitars and harder drums to the song after noticing that the demo had an obvious [pop](/wiki/Pop_music "Pop music") sound. Lyrically, the song is written from a woman's point of view where she expresses her sense of relief with the end of her troubled relationship.

"Since U Been Gone" received universal acclaim from [music critics](/wiki/Music_journalism "Music journalism") who considered the song to be the highlight of *Breakaway*.
